raw.message: Uma horinha atrás eu fiz uma chamada de vídeo com o Fabien. Trocamos altos papos sobre a VM do jogo Another World 😊
Os outros livros do Fabien são muito bons
Ele me disse que "não"... Ele só tá curtindo revisitar o código e dando uma arrumada por que tava meio bagunçado.
pois é... o cara é cauteloso, pra não sair prometendo demais
@fsanches lembrei de você; me passaram um link pro livro Arcade Game Typography
ah, lembrei errado, foi o @villares que mencionou o livro
errou mas acertou. Uma das mil cópias é minha 😃
encontro com ele aproximadamente uma vez por ano em conferencias de tipografia, principalmente na ATypI
eu pensei que seria impossível procurar o livro, mas não, está disponível...
retrocomputacao é nicho. Tipografia é mais nicho ainda. A intersecao dos dois é quase inexistente. Acho que 1000 cópias talvez seja até mesmo um exagero.
a propósito, @fsanches, você continuou algo a parte de vídeo do projeto da placa para o Another World?
conversei com o Fabien Sanglard essa semana e ele me incentivou a retomar esse projeto. Mas não... ainda nao tenho mais nada de avancos para reportar
estou com uma placa de fpga nova aqui para fazer experimentos com saida de video VGA
devo brincar um pouco com isso durante as ferias
Eu terminei fazendo coisas legais aqui; mas não tenho tempo até finais e Dezembro para nada pessoal :(
Estava trabalhando até o mês passado com PCIe.

text.text: Emulating the Original Gameboy’s CPU — Part 2 of a Series
The original DMG CPU clocked at 4.19 MHz
the first part of this series

I’ve been introducing the whole project of building my own version of this iconic handheld gaming console while also discussing some of the requirements to the hardware. Now I’m going to dig in and start working on the heart of the console: the CPU.
In principal, a CPU does the same three steps over and over again: fetch, decode, execute.

To build an emulation of a CPU you basically just need to implement these three steps. First the emulated CPU fetches an operation, then it decodes the operation and finally it executes the operation. After that it’s back to step one.

texts.text: But wait, what does it even mean to fetch an operation? How do you know
to fetch the operation from? And what would such an operation even look like in the first place?

text.text: What an operation looks like is defined by the CPU’s instruction set. Since I’m dealing with an 8 bit CPU here, a typical instruction for the Gameboy consists of eight bits:

texts.text: The above instruction is also known as
and brings all operations on the CPU to a stop until an interrupt occurs (I’ll be talking about what interrupts are later on in this series).

text.text: There are a lot more possible instructions and some of them even take arguments. In order for that to make sense and also to understand how a CPU knows where to fetch operations, it needs some internal memory called registers.

The Gameboy’s CPU is known as the DMG CPU. It is equipped with 6 registers of 16 bit each and they’re called AF, BC, DE, HL, SP and PC. That sounds fairly cryptical, so let’s look at each of them individually.

texts.text:
The AF register is actually more like two 8 bit registers A and F.
A stands for the accumulator and it’s where arithmetic operations usually take place.
F stands for flag register and it’s to be interpreted as 8 distinct bits each with a different meaning. I’ll be looking into this in more detail later.
The BC register is also to be seen as two 8 bit registers B and C. Besides that there’s nothing special about this register.
The DE register is exactly the same as the BC register, just 2x8 bits more to store some data.
The HL register can be used as two 8 bit registers H and L, just like BC and DE. On top of that, it functions as a 16 bit register and can be used to point to addresses in memory.
SP stands for stack pointer. It points to a special area in memory called the stack. More on this later.

The PC register is what I’m interested in right now. It stands for program counter and it’s actually a pointer to the next instruction in memory. And that’s how the CPU knows where to fetch the next operation to be executed.
Now I know what an operation looks like and I know where to find one, or do I? Where do I find the very first instruction? Execution simply starts at location
, that’s where the Gameboy’s boot ROM is located at. My Gameboy won’t incorporate the original boot ROM and start directly with the game. The first instruction for cartridges is at the memory address
(the hexadecimal notation for
). That’s the initial value of my program counter (PC register) and that’s where the CPU is going to look for the first 8 bits of the first operation to be executed.

text.text: I’m talking about fetching instructions from memory but I haven’t even talked about memory itself. That’s okay, though. For now let’s just assume we have some addressable memory and that there’s an actual executable program stored in it. I’ll be talking about memory in more detail in the next post.

The following section is going to include short snippets of C code. I want you to keep in mind that you don’t need to understand the code in order to understand the concepts discussed in this post. You may just skip the code blocks if you’re not used to reading it.

texts.text: I fetched my first 8 bits from the memory address

, next I need to decode the operation. While I’ve seen pretty sophisticated ways the decode CPU instructions, it’s actually very often done using just a single switch/case statement where each operation is its own case.
So let’s say I’ve got some function to fetch 8 bits from memory and store them in a variable called

text.text: I then construct a switch/case to handle each possible operation:

texts.text: Some operations take arguments, for example the operation
takes another 8 bits and adds them to the value stored in register A. So, in case of a
instruction the CPU needs to also fetch the next 8 bits. I can reuse the same
function for that since its only job is to fetch 8 bits from memory.
As you can see, I will have to advance the program counter (PC) by one in order to read the next 8 bits. This is usually done inside the
function, so that every read increments the counter automatically:
With
implemented like that it’s no longer necessary to advance the counter outside of the function.

text.text: Now that instructions can be fetched and decoded, all that’s left to do is to execute them. All a CPU needs for that is access to some memory as well as its internal registers. Let’s have a closer look at the instruction set for the DMG CPU.
These are operations where 8 bits of data are going to be copied from one place to another. Some examples:
Load the contents of one register into another register (e.g. A to B)
Load an arbitrary value of 8 bits into a given register
Load the contents of a location in memory into a register
Load the contents of a register into a location in memory

Although the Gameboy’s CPU is an 8 bit CPU it has some limited ability to work with junks of 16 bit data. All memory addresses are 16 bit long and so is the program counter (PC) and the stack pointer (SP) since they point to locations in memory. In fact, as already mentioned all registers are described as 16 bit registers AF, BC, DE, HL, SP and PC and can be fed directly with 16 bit values. In total there are four 16 bit load commands available:
Load an arbitrary value of 16 bits into a register (e.g. BC)
Load the contents of the HL register into the stack pointer (SP)
Push the contents of a register onto the stack
Pop the contents of the stack into a register

The last two commands may require further explanation. I already introduced the stack pointer register (SP) by mentioning it’s pointing to a special location in memory called the stack. A stack is basically exactly what it sounds like: A place to put some data aside for later use. It’s often used together with branching or subroutines. Those are the times when a program needs to save its registers on the stack before doing something else and popping them off the stack when it’s done.

Besides copying and moving around data, a CPU usually does a lot of arithmetical and logical calculations. It’s no surprise that the DMG CPU has quite a few instructions dedicated to those kinds of tasks:
Adding the value of a given register to the value stored in register A (the accumulator)
Adding an arbitrary value of 8 bits to the value stored in register A
Add the contents of a location in memory to the value stored in register A
The same operations as above but for subtraction instead of addition
Increment or decrement a value stored in a register
Increment or decrement the contents of a location in memory
Logical operations AND, OR, and XOR (exclusive or) of a register with register A
Logical operations AND, OR, and XOR of an arbitrary value with register A
Logical operations AND, OR, and XOR of the contents of a location in memory with register A
Addition and subtraction with respect to certain flags stored in register F
The last point is kind of important and prone to errors, at least in my experience. The flag register (F) holds four flags:

flag for example is being set to

text.text: Remember when you did addition and subtraction by hand in school? You had to carry numbers from one column to the next. That’s exactly what carry means here, too.

text.text: Engenheiro cria cartão de visita eletrônico de US$ 3 com Linux
Cartão de visita de George Hilliard tem USB, roda distribuição Linux e faz boot em 6 segundos; dispositivo usa processador ARM

texts.text: O engenheiro de sistemas embarcados George Hilliard decidiu dar vida nova aos cartões de visita: ele criou um modelo com conectividade USB que roda uma distribuição
e faz boot em cerca de 6 segundos. O dispositivo usa um processador ARM simples importado da China e custa menos de US$ 3.

text.text: Como criar um cartão de visita virtual
Como fazer um cartão de visita no Microsoft Word

texts.text: É possível inserir o cartão em um computador: o boot leva cerca de 6 segundos e, então, você tem acesso a um arquivo leia-me, uma cópia do currículo de Hilliard e algumas fotografias que ele tirou. O shell possui alguns jogos clássicos do Unix, como
e
, além de uma versão simplificada de
e um interpretador da linguagem de programação MicroPython.
O computador roda um firmware personalizado, disponível
; ele foi feito com o Buildroot, uma ferramenta para gerar sistemas Linux embarcados. O
tem 256 KB, o kernel tem 1,6 MB, e todo o sistema de arquivos raiz ocupa 2,4 MB.

text.text: Engenheiro gastou US$ 2,88 em cartão de visita com Linux

texts.text: que o projeto surgiu graças a um interesse em computadores extremamente baratos que conseguem rodar distribuições Linux. Ele começou a pesquisar sobre processadores obscuros e descobriu que alguns modelos “são quase baratos o suficiente para serem distribuídos de graça”. Então, veio a ideia de criar uma placa simples no formato de um cartão de visita.
O processador Allwinner F1C100s
. Ele é muito barato, custando US$ 1,20 na varejista chinesa Taobao; e já vem com 32 MB de
, mais que o suficiente para o que Hilliard planejava.

text.text: O chip da Allwinner é pensado para câmeras de painel de carro (dashcams) e tem arquitetura ARM9; a ARM não lança núcleos com essa tecnologia desde 2006. Isso também não é um problema, já que o foco não está em desempenho.

Hilliard preparou o design do cartão de visita e usou corte a laser em uma placa de circuito impresso. Ele integrou um chip de memória flash de 8 MB, mas o desafio ficou por conta do USB: os conectores precisavam ser longos o bastante para encaixarem na porta.
No total, o engenheiro gastou US$ 2,88 neste projeto. Ele não conta o custo de frete porque fez pedidos de peças para este e outros projetos. Estes são os itens:
